newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Hard sell helps Singapore insurers reach new highs.
newsitem.headline: Hard sell helps Singapore insurers reach new highs.

text.p: The reform of Singapore's state pension scheme and aggressive selling are the driving forces behind a surge in new life insurance policies sold in the city-state, a senior industry executive said on Tuesday.
"Agents are aggressively well-trained to reach out to customers and convince them of the importance of life insurance," Eric Seah, chief actuary with Great Eastern Life, told Reuters.
Reform of the Central Provident Fund (CPF) pension scheme, allowing individuals to use their funds to buy private sector investment instruments, also helped, Seah said.
"The CPF liberalisation of rules also fuelled the growth of endowment and single premium plans," he said in a written reply to questions.

The number of life insurance policies in force in Singapore almost doubled between 1992 and 1996 to 2.8 million from 1.5 million, the Monetary Authority of Singapore said in its first monthly statistical bulletin of 1997.
Premiums for individual life insurance policies soared from Singapore $1.6 billion (US$1.1 billion) to S$3.4 billion over the period, said the report from the de facto central bank.
The total value of Singaporean lives assured by the local industry now tops S$134.5 billion.
Insurers predict S$2.0 billion could be sunk into insurance and investment products over the next three years following the second of a three-stage reform of CPF that took effect on January 1 1997.
About S$1.0 billion of CPF funds has been invested in insurance products since the first reforms of the compulsory savings scheme began in 1993.
A final factor helping push the level of sales to their new high was a good level of return on investment, Seah said.
"The prevailing low interest rate of traditional savings mediums like band and fixed deposits spur many (people) to look for alternative mediums with better returns.
"Endowment insurance, for example, offers a yield of about four percent to five percent, higher than the three percent offered by banks," he said.
